claims.text: Enhanced free-energy sampling can be integrated with molecular dynamics simulations for high-entropy alloys.

Enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics will accurately and efficiently compute melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a broad range of HEA compositions.
The intended initial material is a disordered, single-phase crystalline HEA at room temperature.
Enhanced free-energy sampling effectively overcomes free-energy barriers during solid-to-liquid transitions.
The simulations can be performed near melting under equilibrium conditions while systematically varying temperature, pressure, and composition.
Mapping the free-energy surface will capture barrier crossings and solid-to-liquid transition pathways.
Conventional molecular dynamics is limited in its ability to explore rare events and barrier crossings relevant to HEA melting.
Enhanced sampling explores rare events and barrier crossings more efficiently than conventional molecular dynamics.
Improved barrier crossing enables precise determination of latent heat, entropy change, and volume change at melting.
Predicted melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies and entropies, and melting volume changes will agree with experiments within approximately 5–10%.
Enhanced-sampling simulations will significantly outperform standard molecular dynamics in both accuracy and computational time.
Standard molecular dynamics typically has errors of approximately 20% or more for rapid HEA phase transitions.
Standard molecular dynamics is less efficient than enhanced sampling for capturing rapid HEA phase transitions.
The approach should perform well for disordered, single-phase HEAs.
Significant ordering, phase separation, or complex intermetallic formation may limit the approach.
Exact error margins and computational-efficiency gains across the HEA compositional space are not yet established.
Calorimetry, DSC, dilatometry, and in situ X-ray diffraction can provide experimental reference values for the proposed melting quantities.
Disagreement greater than approximately 10% for the specified melting properties across a majority of tested HEAs would falsify the claimed accuracy.
